docs.title: octools
docs.text:
Version: 1.2.1 · Date: 2026-10-08

octools is the OpsCogs standard interface for AI agent tools, in Python and TypeScript.

It holds the OCTool descriptor, the result envelopes every tool returns, a conformance validator, and plain-data converters to the MCP and Anthropic tool shapes. A library describes each capability once as an OCTool; any agent runtime registers it without re-expressing it by hand.

Think of it as OpenAPI for agent tools: one vendor-neutral contract that every OpsCogs library fills in, so the interface is defined once and each adopter only supplies its tools. The contract ships as two packages with the same API, one per language:

Language Package Runtime Only dependency Python octools on PyPI Python 3.12 or newer pydantic >= 2.12, < 3 TypeScript @opscogs/octools on npm Node 22.18 or newer, ESM only zod 4, a peer dependency

Neither package depends on an OpsCogs package or an agent SDK, so the dependency arrow always points toward octools, never back. The source for both lives in one repository: github.com/opscogs/octools.

  • The OCTool descriptor - every field, the envelopes, the escape conditions, strict-clean rules, versioning.
  • Converters - the MCP and Anthropic mappings, what is lossless and what is dropped.
  • Listing tools for people - the octools list command and the listing API behind it.
  • The TypeScript package - runtime floor, the Python to TypeScript name map, and where the two languages differ.
  • TypeScript API - the generated reference for every export of @opscogs/octools.

Code examples on these pages come in both languages. Pick a tab once and every page follows it.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
PythonTypeScript

Python 3.12 or newer and pydantic >= 2.12, < 3 (the only dependency).

pip install octools

Node 22.18 or newer; the package is ESM only and ships its type declarations. zod 4 is a peer dependency, so install it beside the package.

npm install @opscogs/octools zod

docs.title: One contract, two languages
docs.text:
The wire format is defined once, outside either package, in the repository's spec/ directory:

  • vocabulary.json - SPEC_VERSION, every closed vocabulary with its declared fallback, and the shared constants (name patterns, sentence limits, the strict-mode keyword and format sets).
  • schema/*.schema.json - the JSON Schemas of the descriptor and the envelopes.
  • fixtures/<operation>/<case>.json - golden cases, one per file, each with an input and the expected result. An error or a validator finding is data in expected, never a language's exception type.

Both packages' test suites run every fixture and pass all of them; none is skipped or filtered by language. Conforming to octools means passing spec/, so the same envelope, the same findings and the same converter output come back whichever package produced them. Wire keys are spelled exactly as the spec spells them in both (column_kinds, next_cursor, inputSchema); only the API names follow each language's idiom.

Versions move in lockstep. One release tag publishes both packages at the same version, recorded in one changelog, and SPEC_VERSION is the same in both. A pre-release is spelled 1.2.0rc1 on PyPI and 1.2.0-rc.1 on npm, where it is published under the next tag and never installed by default. The compatibility contract in Versioning and deprecation applies to both registries identically: a consuming library declares a range from the oldest release carrying every name it uses up to the next major.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Describe the arguments and result as models, wrap the function in an OCTool, and list the tools from the provider function (all_tools() in Python, allTools() in TypeScript):

PythonTypeScript 
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from octools import OCTool, RecordsEnvelope, input_schema_for, records_schema


class EchoArgs(BaseModel):
    values: list[str] = Field(description="Strings to echo back, one record each.")


class EchoRecord(BaseModel):
    value: str = Field(description="The echoed string.")
    position: int = Field(description="Zero-based position in the input.")


def echo_records(_dependency, *, values: list[str]) -> dict:
    records = [EchoRecord(value=v, position=i) for i, v in enumerate(values)]
    return RecordsEnvelope[EchoRecord](
        records=records, count=len(records), truncated=False
    ).model_dump(mode="json")


ECHO_RECORDS = OCTool(
    name="echo_records",
    description="Return each input string as one record with its position. Use it to check a tool round-trip. Returns a records envelope.",
    input_schema=input_schema_for(EchoArgs),
    output_schema=records_schema(EchoRecord),
    func=echo_records,
    access="local",
)


def all_tools() -> tuple[OCTool, ...]:
    return (ECHO_RECORDS,)

// src/my_tools.ts
import * as z from "zod";
import {
  OCTool,
  RecordsEnvelope,
  inputSchemaFor,
  recordsSchema,
} from "@opscogs/octools";

const EchoArgs = z.object({
  values: z.array(z.string()).describe("Strings to echo back, one record each."),
});

const EchoRecord = z
  .object({
    value: z.string().describe("The echoed string."),
    position: z.int().describe("Zero-based position in the input."),
  })
  .meta({ id: "EchoRecord" });

function echoRecords(_dependency: unknown, args: unknown): RecordsEnvelope {
  const { values } = EchoArgs.parse(args);
  const records = values.map((value, position) => ({ value, position }));
  return RecordsEnvelope(EchoRecord).parse({
    records,
    count: records.length,
    truncated: false,
  });
}

export const ECHO_RECORDS = new OCTool({
  name: "echo_records",
  description:
    "Return each input string as one record with its position. Use it to check a tool round-trip. Returns a records envelope.",
  inputSchema: inputSchemaFor(EchoArgs),
  outputSchema: recordsSchema(EchoRecord),
  func: echoRecords,
  access: "local",
});

export function allTools(): readonly OCTool[] {
  return [ECHO_RECORDS];
}

.meta({ id }) puts the record model in $defs, as pydantic does for a nested model, so both packages emit the same output schema. A parse returns the envelope's wire form, ready for JSON.stringify.

Assert conformance in your own test suite, not at import time:

PythonTypeScript 
# tests/test_conformance.py
from octools import validate_provider
import my_tools


def test_conformance():
    assert validate_provider(my_tools) == []

// test/conformance.test.ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { validateProvider } from "@opscogs/octools";
import * as myTools from "../src/my_tools.js";

test("conformance", () => {
  expect(validateProvider(myTools)).toEqual([]);
});

The converters then give a runtime the registration objects it needs: to_mcp_tool(ECHO_RECORDS) and to_anthropic_tool(ECHO_RECORDS, name_prefix="demo_") in Python, toMcpTool(ECHO_RECORDS) and toAnthropicTool(ECHO_RECORDS, { namePrefix: "demo_" }) in TypeScript; see Converters.

docs.title: Converters
docs.text:
Version: 1.2.0 · Date: 2026-10-08

The converters turn an OCTool into the registration object a target expects, as plain data: dicts in Python, plain objects in TypeScript. No SDK is imported, so a library can test its descriptors without depending on mcp or anthropic (or @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and @anthropic-ai/sdk). Lossless round-trip is the design goal; where a target has no slot for a field the mapping says so here. Both packages produce the same output for the same descriptor, key for key.

PythonTypeScript 
from octools import to_anthropic_tool, to_mcp_tool
from my_tools import ECHO_RECORDS

mcp_tool = to_mcp_tool(ECHO_RECORDS, name_prefix="site_a_")
anthropic_tool = to_anthropic_tool(ECHO_RECORDS, name_prefix="demo_")

import { toAnthropicTool, toMcpTool } from "@opscogs/octools";
import { ECHO_RECORDS } from "./my_tools.js";

const mcpTool = toMcpTool(ECHO_RECORDS, { namePrefix: "site_a_" });
const anthropicTool = toAnthropicTool(ECHO_RECORDS, { namePrefix: "demo_" });

The tables below name the Python descriptor fields; the TypeScript OCTool has the same fields in camelCase (input_schema is inputSchema, read_only_hint is readOnlyHint). The output keys are identical in both. A prefixed name that breaks the target's pattern raises OCToolError in both packages.

docs.title: MCP: to_mcp_tool(tool, *, name_prefix="")
docs.text:
TypeScript: toMcpTool(tool, { namePrefix }).

Produces an MCP Tool object (specification 2025-11-25 and 2026-07-28; the Tool object and its name rule are unchanged between them for the fields this mapping uses). Everything but func survives, because func is the server's handler rather than protocol data.

OCTool field MCP field name name, with name_prefix prepended; the result must match MCP_NAME_RE (^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,128}$) or OCToolError is raised title title (only when set) description description input_schema inputSchema (verbatim copy) output_schema outputSchema (verbatim copy, only when set) read_only_hint annotations.readOnlyHint destructive_hint annotations.destructiveHint idempotent_hint annotations.idempotentHint access _meta["com.opscogs.octools/access"] target _meta["com.opscogs.octools/target"] (only when set) result_kind _meta["com.opscogs.octools/result_kind"] deprecated _meta["com.opscogs.octools/deprecated"] meta _meta["com.opscogs.octools/meta"] (copy) SPEC_VERSION _meta["com.opscogs.octools/spec_version"]

_meta keys use the reverse-DNS prefix com.opscogs.octools/ per the MCP _meta convention, so they never collide with another vendor's keys. The package label sits in the prefix because MCP allows only a single slash per key, and other OpsCogs packages use their own com.opscogs.<package>/ prefix. openWorldHint is not emitted: it has no clean OpsCogs meaning yet. Schemas are deep copies, so a consumer can decorate the result without touching the descriptor.

Example:

{
  "name": "cluster_info",
  "title": "Cluster identity and versions",
  "description": "...",
  "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": {}, "additionalProperties": false },
  "outputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": {} },
  "annotations": { "readOnlyHint": true, "destructiveHint": false, "idempotentHint": true },
  "_meta": {
    "com.opscogs.octools/spec_version": "1.1",
    "com.opscogs.octools/access": "remote",
    "com.opscogs.octools/result_kind": "records",
    "com.opscogs.octools/deprecated": false,
    "com.opscogs.octools/meta": { "min_api_version": "2.10" },
    "com.opscogs.octools/target": "cluster"
  }
}

name_prefix (namePrefix) has the same meaning as on to_anthropic_tool: a server that publishes one provider against two targets passes a different prefix per target (site_a_, site_b_) so the names do not collide. The prefix is not recorded in _meta; the server that added it strips it before dispatching to func.

The reverse mapping is mechanical, and the test suite proves it: an OCTool rebuilt from to_mcp_tool(tool) plus the original func compares equal to tool.

docs.title: Anthropic: to_anthropic_tool(tool, *, name_prefix="")
docs.text:
TypeScript: toAnthropicTool(tool, { namePrefix }).

Produces a Messages API tools[] entry with exactly three keys.

OCTool field Anthropic field name name, with name_prefix prepended; the result must match ANTHROPIC_NAME_RE (^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,128}$) or OCToolError is raised description description input_schema input_schema, with every title and x- key stripped at schema level and additionalProperties: false added to the root if missing

The runtime supplies the namespace prefix (demo_, for example), which is why descriptor names stop at 48 characters. Property names are never altered, even one literally called title.

Dropped, because the API has no slot for them: title, output_schema, the three hints, access and target, result_kind, deprecated, meta, and func. A runtime keeps those in its own registry, which is where approval policy, result rendering and deprecation warnings already read them. strict is not emitted either: turning strict mode on is a runtime decision, and a strict-clean input schema is what makes it possible.

{
  "name": "demo_cluster_info",
  "description": "...",
  "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": {}, "additionalProperties": false }
}

docs.title: Other targets
docs.text: OpenAI function tools want every property in required and optionals as type: ["string", "null"]; pydantic-ai and LangChain accept the 2020-12 schema as is. Those transforms are consumer-side, not this package's; input_schema is the stable input to all of them.

docs.title: The OCTool descriptor
docs.text:
Version: 1.2.0 · Date: 2026-10-08

OCTool is a frozen descriptor of one capability a library offers to an agent runtime: a keyword-only dataclass in Python, a class built with new OCTool({ ... }) in TypeScript. This page is the reference: every field, the result envelopes, when a tool may skip a result schema, what "strict-clean" means for an input schema, and how the format and the tools themselves evolve. octools.SPEC_VERSION is "1.1".

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Construction validates the structural rules below and raises OCToolError on the first failure (a ValueError in Python, an Error subclass in TypeScript). Policy rules (marked validator) are reported as findings by validate_tool and validate_provider instead, so a library can list every problem at once.

Field Type Default Meaning name str required Matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,47}$: lowercase snake_case, at most 48 characters, leaving room for a runtime prefix under the tightest common name limit (64). description str required Written for a model to read: what it does, when not to use it, what it returns, one caveat. Two to four sentences (validator); avoid abbreviations such as e.g., the sentence counter splits on . followed by a space. input_schema Mapping[str, Any] required JSON Schema 2020-12 with an object root, generated from a pydantic model by input_schema_for. Must be strict-clean (validator). func Callable[..., Any] required func(dependency, **args): the injected dependency first (a client, a workspace, a sink), validated keyword arguments after. Returns a JSON object. access "local" or "remote" required Where the tool acts: in-process data or a remote system of record. remote means the tool reaches that system through its injected dependency, so a runtime applies its remote policy (approval, timeouts, audit) to the call. target str \| None None Optional free-text label for the access target a library fills in, for example "cluster". output_schema Mapping[str, Any] \| None None JSON Schema 2020-12 for the result, generated by output_schema_for. Preferred, not mandatory: see Escape conditions (validator). result_kind "records" or "artifact" "records" Which envelope the result uses, so a runtime knows whether to read the result or to embed and cite it. title str \| None None Optional human label (MCP title). read_only_hint bool True MCP readOnlyHint. Describes the access target, not the filesystem: writing through an injected sink is still read-only with respect to the system of record. destructive_hint bool False MCP destructiveHint; meaningful when not read-only. idempotent_hint bool True MCP idempotentHint; meaningful when not read-only. deprecated bool False An alias kept alive after a rename; must name the replacement in meta["alias_of"] (validator). meta Mapping[str, Any] {} Library facts the consumer may read, plain snake_case keys: min_api_version, schema_escape, alias_of. Exported to MCP under _meta["com.opscogs.octools/meta"].

The table gives the Python names and types. In TypeScript every field is camelCase (input_schema is inputSchema, read_only_hint is readOnlyHint, result_kind is resultKind), a schema or meta is a plain object, an unset optional field reads as null, and an unknown field in the constructor argument raises OCToolError.

Hints are advisory. They inform a runtime's approval policy; they never replace it, and a runtime must treat them as untrusted unless it trusts the library.

docs.title: The callable contract
docs.text:
func takes the injected dependency positionally and validated keyword arguments. It validates its own inputs (a pydantic model is the usual way), does no I/O beyond the dependency, reads no environment, never prints, never exits, and lets library exceptions propagate so the caller maps them. Invalid arguments raise ValueError (pydantic's ValidationError is one); in TypeScript, parsing the arguments with the tool's zod schema throws ZodError. Numeric bounds such as "1 to 100" live in the description and in this validation, not in the schema. TypeScript's ToolFunc leaves the parameter list to the runtime; the examples on this site follow the same contract with the arguments as one object, func(dependency, args).

func is a plain synchronous callable. Construction raises OCToolError for a coroutine or async function or an async-generator function. An async or streaming variant, when one is needed, arrives as a separate optional field that an older runtime ignores, never as a change to func itself.

docs.title: For runtime authors
docs.text: A runtime looks a tool up by name in all_tools() (allTools() in TypeScript), validates the arguments against input_schema (or lets the tool do it, since it always validates its own), and calls func(dependency, **args). The dependency is whatever the library documents for its tools; pass None when it documents that none is needed. The result is a JSON object and, when output_schema is present, conforms to it. to_mcp_tool and to_anthropic_tool drop func, so the runtime keeps the descriptor for dispatch. validate_provider takes a provider object or module with an all_tools() method, not a list (a list raises AttributeError), and calls all_tools() twice to check that the order is stable. In TypeScript a module namespace (import * as myTools) with an exported allTools function is a provider.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
A library exposes all_tools() returning its descriptors in a fixed order with unique names; ToolProvider is the protocol (an interface in TypeScript), and a module with an all_tools function (allTools) satisfies it. validate_provider calls it twice and reports unstable_order or duplicate_name. MCP asks for deterministic listings so prompt caches stay warm.

A runtime that registers more than one library's tools validates the union, not each half: a name two libraries share is only visible there. merge_providers(*providers) (mergeProviders(...providers)) returns a provider whose all_tools() concatenates theirs in argument order. It deduplicates nothing on purpose, so a collision comes back as a duplicate_name finding instead of one tool quietly winning.

PythonTypeScript 
from octools import merge_providers, validate_provider
import my_tools
import partner_tools

registered = merge_providers(my_tools, partner_tools)
assert validate_provider(registered) == []

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { mergeProviders, validateProvider } from "@opscogs/octools";
import * as myTools from "./my_tools.js";
import * as partnerTools from "./partner_tools.js";

const registered = mergeProviders(myTools, partnerTools);
assert.deepEqual(validateProvider(registered), []);

docs.title: Result envelopes
docs.text:
A result is always a JSON object. Three models define the shapes: pydantic models in Python, zod schemas in TypeScript. Their JSON Schemas come from records_schema(Item), tabular_schema() and artifact_schema() (recordsSchema(item), tabularSchema(), artifactSchema()).

Records (result_kind="records"), for results whose record shape is known in advance:

{ "records": [{ "...": "keys follow the item schema" }], "count": 12, "truncated": false }

A page of a longer result adds the optional paging fields:

{ "records": ["..."], "count": 2, "truncated": true, "total_count": 3, "next_cursor": "...", "resumable": true }

RecordsEnvelope[Item] is generic over the item model; in TypeScript, RecordsEnvelope(item) returns the schema over records that item parses. truncated is true when a cap, a stop or an interrupted read cut the list short; count is the number returned and must equal the length of records, or the envelope rejects it. total_count is optional: the exact size of the full result when the source knows it, omitted when unknown or approximate. It is int | str | None: a JSON integer up to 2^53 - 1, or - above that - a non-negative decimal string (^(0|[1-9][0-9]*)$), the same rule as the big_integer column kind (below); a producer may send a string for any value, and a reader compares it numerically, never lexically. next_cursor is optional: an opaque token present only when truncated is true. stop_reason is optional: why a truncated read stopped early. resumable is computed, true exactly when next_cursor is present, and in the serialized JSON only when truncated is true (see Paging). warnings is optional: non-fatal problems the caller should relay, one string per entry (see Warnings on list envelopes). The optional fields are left out of the serialized JSON when absent, and warnings when empty; model_dump does this itself, so a tool never needs exclude_none. In TypeScript a parse (RecordsEnvelope(item).parse(data)) returns that serialized form directly, ready for JSON.stringify.

Tabular, for results whose columns are only known at run time (an ad-hoc SQL result). There is no tabular result_kind: a tabular tool keeps result_kind="records" and a runtime detects the shape from the columns and rows properties of its output schema.

{
  "columns": ["host", "count"],
  "rows": [["a", 1]],
  "row_count": 1,
  "truncated": false,
  "column_kinds": ["fqdn", "integer"]
}

TabularEnvelope takes columns, rows, row_count, truncated, and optionally column_kinds, column_scales, column_descriptions, total_count, next_cursor, stop_reason and warnings; a truncated envelope's dump adds the computed resumable. Cells are scalars, Cell = str | int | float | bool | None (string | number | boolean | null in TypeScript), and row_count must equal the length of rows. A tabular tool declares tabular_schema() as its output schema:

PythonTypeScript 
from octools import OCTool, TabularEnvelope, input_schema_for, tabular_schema


def host_table(_dependency, *, region: str) -> dict:
    rows = [[h["host"], h["cores"]] for h in HOSTS if h["region"] == region]
    return TabularEnvelope(
        columns=["host", "cores"],
        rows=rows,
        row_count=len(rows),
        truncated=False,
        column_kinds=["fqdn", "integer"],
    ).model_dump(mode="json")


HOST_TABLE = OCTool(
    name="host_table",
    description="...",
    input_schema=input_schema_for(QueryArgs),
    output_schema=tabular_schema(),
    func=host_table,
    access="local",
)

import {
  OCTool,
  TabularEnvelope,
  inputSchemaFor,
  tabularSchema,
} from "@opscogs/octools";

function hostTable(_dependency: unknown, args: unknown): TabularEnvelope {
  const { region } = QueryArgs.parse(args);
  const rows = HOSTS.filter((h) => h.region === region).map((h) => [
    h.host,
    h.cores,
  ]);
  return TabularEnvelope.parse({
    columns: ["host", "cores"],
    rows,
    row_count: rows.length,
    truncated: false,
    column_kinds: ["fqdn", "integer"],
  });
}

export const HOST_TABLE = new OCTool({
  name: "host_table",
  description: "...",
  inputSchema: inputSchemaFor(QueryArgs),
  outputSchema: tabularSchema(),
  func: hostTable,
  access: "local",
});

column_kinds is optional, one entry per column, drawn from the closed vocabulary COLUMN_KINDS (ColumnKind is the matching Literal, or union type in TypeScript, ten kinds); any other value is a validation error on construction, model_validate or a TypeScript .parse. Like the other optional envelope fields, it is left out of the serialized JSON when absent. The kinds are what a renderer needs to align, format or chart a column, and each maps onto a JSON Schema type or format:

Kind JSON Schema Render text string - number number - integer integer - boolean boolean - timestamp string, format date-time - ip string, format ipv4 or ipv6 - fqdn string, format hostname - mac string - ip_block string: an address, a CIDR prefix, or a first-last range monospace, left-aligned big_integer integer, or string of decimal digits with an optional - right-aligned

Kinds are not JSON Schema format names: write fqdn and ip, not hostname or ipv4, which belong to an input schema's format.

ip_block holds any contiguous set of addresses in one family, written as a bare address (a block of one), address/length, or first-last; a column that only ever holds single addresses stays ip. big_integer holds an integer of any size: a cell is a JSON integer when its magnitude fits in 2^53 - 1 and a decimal string otherwise, so a reader never loses precision and a small value never needs parsing. Parsing never checks a cell against its declared kind - that is validate_tabular, below.

docs.title: column_scales
docs.text:
column_scales is optional, one entry per column, parallel to columns and column_kinds: list[ColumnScale | None] | None, drawn from the closed vocabulary COLUMN_SCALES (ColumnScale is the matching Literal or union type, "linear" | "log10" | "log2"). TabularEnvelope rejects a column_scales list of the wrong length. A non-None entry requires column_kinds to be present and that column's kind to be number, integer or big_integer; any other combination is a validation error on construction or model_validate, since a scale on an fqdn column has no sensible reading. A tolerant reader relaxes this one cross-field check: read_envelope (below) reads a scale on a column whose kind is non-numeric, whose kind degraded to text, or where column_kinds is absent altogether, as None rather than rejecting the envelope. Omitted, or None for one column, the envelope serializes exactly as before and a renderer applies its own data-driven rule (below).

{
  "columns": ["prefix", "prefix_len", "size"],
  "column_kinds": ["ip_block", "integer", "big_integer"],
  "column_scales": [null, null, "log2"],
  "rows": [
    ["2001:db8::/32", 32, "79228162514264337593543950336"],
    ["2001:db8::/64", 64, "18446744073709551616"]
  ],
  "row_count": 2,
  "truncated": false
}

docs.title: column_descriptions
docs.text:
column_descriptions is optional, one entry per column, parallel to columns: list[str | None] | None, a short description of what each column holds, None for a column with none. It gives a schema-less tabular result (an ad-hoc query over terse source column names) the meaning a records tool gets from its item schema's field descriptions. TabularEnvelope rejects a list of the wrong length, and the field is left out of the serialized JSON when absent. read_envelope drops a malformed column_descriptions - not a list, the wrong length, or an entry that is neither a string nor null - and reads the rest of the envelope, since a description is a hint and always safe to drop.

A paged producer may send column_descriptions on the first page only, to save tokens: the columns do not change between pages, so a caller keeps the descriptions it was first given.

{
  "columns": ["hn", "vc"],
  "column_descriptions": ["Host name.", "Virtual CPU count."],
  "rows": [["a", 4]],
  "row_count": 1,
  "truncated": false
}

docs.title: Renderer guidance
docs.text:
A renderer charting a numeric column never rewrites the cell - the envelope stays exact end to end - and prints the original cell for every value a person reads (table cells, tooltips, data labels, exports), sorting a big_integer column by BigInt(cell) while plotting Number(cell): a JavaScript float64 carries enough significant digits that plotting it is visually exact even at 2^128, so precision is never the reason to avoid a linear axis.

  • A declared scale wins: log2 draws a log axis ticked at whole powers of two (2^0, 2^32, 2^64, ...); log10 ticks at powers of ten; linear stays linear even when the range is wide.
  • With no declared scale, a renderer uses a logarithmic axis when every plotted value is positive and the largest is at least 1000 times the smallest, and linear otherwise, falling back to linear when a value is zero or negative.
  • Base-10 ticks format compactly (3.4 x 10^38); exact values stay in tooltips and labels, never in the plotted or tick data itself.
  • A renderer that cannot draw a given scale, or is not charting at all, ignores column_scales.

docs.title: validate_tabular
Paging
docs.text:
truncated says a list was cut short; next_cursor says how to continue; resumable says whether continuing is possible; stop_reason says what stopped the read early. A tool that can continue sets next_cursor to an opaque token and the caller passes it back unchanged as the tool's cursor argument. The convention for a paged tool's input is an optional cursor: str | None (omit for the first page) and limit: int, with the bounds in the description as usual. A list tool that never continues a read takes no cursor, even though its envelope schema carries next_cursor, so the validator does not check the pairing; a producer's own test does, by passing each next_cursor back as cursor until the last page has none. Cursor contents are private to the tool; a caller never parses them. There is no offset: cursor paging is modelled on the nextCursor MCP uses for its own list operations (no protocol defines paging for a tool's result), stays stable while data is appended, and asks the model only to echo a token rather than do arithmetic.

resumable is a computed field: true exactly when next_cursor is present, so the two never disagree. It answers the question truncated alone does not, whether following the read is possible, so it is serialized only when truncated is true, where it is always present, true or false. A complete read's dump leaves it out and has the same keys as a 1.0 dump, so it still passes a 1.0-built consumer's closed input schema. A reader treats an absent resumable as false:

truncated resumable Meaning true true There is more; call again with next_cursor as cursor. true false The read ended for good; calling again with the same arguments serves the same items. stop_reason says why. false absent A complete read.

These dump and schema rules apply to the resumable that RecordsEnvelope and TabularEnvelope define. A subclass that defines its own resumable computed field keeps the output shape such a subclass had under 1.0: its dump carries resumable always, true or false, and its output schema lists it as required. Its input-mode schema declares resumable as an optional boolean, so its dump passes an envelope-typed closed input schema. model_validate still accepts a resumable key on every subclass and checks it against next_cursor.

stop_reason is a free string, omitted when the read ended naturally or the caller's limit simply cut it. It is not a closed vocabulary, so it has no fallback and a reader shows an unfamiliar value as it stands. The well-known values include:

stop_reason The read stopped because run_deadline the run's time budget ran out; the items collected so far are returned page_count it reached the configured cap on source pages per read record_limit it stopped at a record or row cap; with no next_cursor when the producer cannot resume past it, such as a server-side row cap on a query interrupted the process running it was interrupted partway cursor_stalled the source handed back the cursor it was given, so following it would serve the same items again; no next_cursor is published

Both list envelopes reject a next_cursor or a stop_reason when truncated is false, and a total_count smaller than the number returned. A dumped envelope validates again: model_validate (and read_envelope) accepts a resumable key, checks it against next_cursor and does not store it, so model_validate(env.model_dump()) round-trips. A resumable that contradicts next_cursor raises in both, since it is corrupt data, not a newer producer. records_schema(Item) and tabular_schema() describe the dumped shape: resumable is an optional boolean property and stop_reason an optional string one. A tool's input schema that nests an envelope by $ref (input_schema_for on a model with a TabularEnvelope or RecordsEnvelope field) declares the same optional resumable, so any dump passes it unchanged under additionalProperties: false. A tool validates the cursor it receives like any other argument: the reference implementation rejects a negative or non-numeric cursor with a ValueError naming cursor. Decision record OCTL-0002 records the choice.

docs.title: Warnings on list envelopes
docs.text:
RecordsEnvelope and TabularEnvelope carry warnings: list[str], with the same meaning as on ArtifactEnvelope: non-fatal problems the caller should relay, one per entry, beside a result that is still usable. A read over several sources reports a source that failed or lacked a table this way instead of failing the whole call. warnings defaults to empty and the list envelopes leave an empty list out of the serialized JSON, so a result with no warnings keeps the 1.0 shape; ArtifactEnvelope always serializes its warnings, empty or not.

{
  "columns": ["snapshot", "hosts"],
  "rows": [["a", 12]],
  "row_count": 1,
  "truncated": false,
  "warnings": ["snapshot b has no table hosts"]
}

Artifact (result_kind="artifact"), for tools that produce a file:

{
  "artifact": { "reference": "reports/assets/a1.svg", "media_type": "image/svg+xml", "bytes": 2048, "width": 640, "height": 360 },
  "artifacts": [],
  "warnings": [],
  "sensitivity": "inherits_input"
}

reference is whatever the injected sink returned; the library never chooses a filename. role says what the artifact is to the run, such as csv, plan or summary; it is free text, not a closed vocabulary, so it has no fallback. width, height and role are omitted when unset, as is every optional envelope field left at None. artifacts lists further outputs beside the primary. sensitivity is "inherits_input" today: per-field extras cannot annotate a file, so redaction and audit layers treat the artifact as containing every input column. The vocabulary may gain a value later, but only one less restrictive than "inherits_input", which stays the fallback a tolerant reader gives an unrecognized value (see Reading envelopes from another process).

docs.title: Sensitivity on record fields
docs.text:
Per-field sensitivity goes on the result model only, as a pydantic json_schema_extra or a zod .meta() key, under an x- key: {"x-sensitivity": "identifier" | "free_text" | "none" | "secret"}. The x- prefix follows OpenAPI's extension rule so no future JSON Schema keyword collides, and keeping it off input schemas means nothing unknown is ever sent to a strict-mode API.

PythonTypeScript 
class HostRecord(BaseModel):
    host: str = Field(
        description="Host name.", json_schema_extra={"x-sensitivity": "identifier"}
    )
    cores: int = Field(description="Number of CPU cores.")

const HostRecord = z.object({
  host: z
    .string()
    .meta({ description: "Host name.", "x-sensitivity": "identifier" }),
  cores: z.int().describe("Number of CPU cores."),
});

The four values are a convention for redaction and audit layers; the validator does not check them. secret is the most sensitive value: a redaction or audit layer that meets an x-sensitivity value it does not recognize treats it as secret, since nothing enforces this convention and the only safe reading of an unknown marker is the most restrictive one.

docs.title: Reading envelopes from another process
Escape conditions
docs.text:
output_schema is preferred, not mandatory. It may be None, or an open object (additionalProperties: true with the always-present keys listed in required), only when:

  1. the tool is a raw pass-through whose keys the caller chooses (a generic object read with _return_fields);
  2. the shape depends on a per-instance schema fetched at run time (object-type discovery);
  3. the source is schema-less (free-form SQL) - use the tabular envelope.

The escape must be explicit: record the reason as a non-empty string in meta["schema_escape"], or the validator reports output_schema_escape. That rule fires on a missing schema or a root with a literal additionalProperties: true; the envelopes are closed because they forbid extra fields, and a hand-rolled output model should do the same. When a schema is present the result must conform to it (MCP's rule). The escape covers output schemas only: an input schema has no escape because strict-mode model APIs reject an open object outright, so a free-form options argument must be modelled as a closed object.

docs.title: Strict-clean input schemas
docs.text:
Input schemas are sent to model APIs with strict: true, so they must stay inside the keyword subset both Anthropic and OpenAI accept. input_schema_for(Model) (inputSchemaFor(schema)) produces such a schema from a plain pydantic model or zod object; strict_clean(schema) (strictClean) reports every violation as a Finding with a JSON pointer path and never mutates the schema. A zod string format such as z.iso.datetime() also emits a pattern, which strictClean reports; declare an input format as z.string().meta({ format: "date-time" }) instead.

  • Object root; additionalProperties: false on every object schema.
  • Keywords: type, properties, required, additionalProperties, items, enum, const, anyOf, allOf, $ref, $defs, default, description, format, minItems. Nothing else: no title, no x- keys, no minimum / maximum / minLength / maxLength / pattern, no oneOf.
  • Types: object, array, string, integer, number, boolean, null. Optional fields are anyOf: [{type}, {type: null}] with default: null and omitted from required.
  • Formats: date-time, time, date, duration, email, hostname, uri, ipv4, ipv6, uuid.
  • minItems only 0 or 1; enum values primitives.
  • $ref only to a root $defs entry, never inside allOf, never recursive.

Output schemas are unconstrained 2020-12 (nothing sends them to a grammar compiler), which is where x-sensitivity and any bounds belong. A free-form dict field is an open object and therefore not strict-clean; model it as a closed object or move it out of the input schema.

docs.title: Versioning and deprecation
docs.text: SPEC_VERSION is "1.1", the format version of the descriptor and the envelopes. Under the compatibility contract below, a spec minor is additive and a spec major is one of the "must not" changes. A reader checks the major only; a test that pins the whole string fails on every spec minor. The spec version and the package version are independent: a release that adds a helper leaves SPEC_VERSION alone.

docs.title: The compatibility contract
docs.text:
Every release within a major follows one rule for producers and readers: a reader that drops an addition, or reads it as its declared fallback, still reads the rest of the envelope or descriptor correctly. An addition that fails this test needs a new major.

A minor release may add:

  • an optional envelope or descriptor field whose absence means exactly what it meant before;
  • a vocabulary value whose fallback reading is safe (a sensitivity value only when it is less restrictive than "inherits_input");
  • a function, a helper or an export;
  • a new validate_tool, validate_provider or strict_clean rule, or a tighter existing one (a smaller strict-clean keyword set, a lower sentence-count ceiling, a stricter name pattern) - shipped opt-in, the way validate_tabular does, since a default-on new rule would break a consumer's validate_provider(p) == [] assertion. Loosening a rule is allowed in a minor without the opt-in requirement;
  • a key in to_mcp_tool or to_anthropic_tool output (openWorldHint, icons, input_examples), or in a dumped envelope and its schema (the computed resumable) - a consumer asserts on the keys it needs, not on whole-dict equality. An envelope key added in a minor is left out of the dump when it carries nothing new (resumable on a complete read, an empty list-envelope warnings), so a result that does not use it keeps the older shape and passes an older consumer's closed input schema;
  • an optional field on Finding, defaulting to None.

A release must not, before a new major:

  • remove or rename a field, value or export;
  • make an optional field required;
  • change what an existing field or value means, or what an existing converter output key means, or remove one;
  • add a field a reader must understand to read the rest correctly (for example, a flag meaning "rows are deltas" would silently corrupt a tolerant reader);
  • add a vocabulary value whose fallback reading is less safe than the value itself (a sensitivity value more restrictive than "inherits_input");
  • tighten a check on parse - an opt-in check such as validate_tabular is fine, since nothing calls it implicitly;
  • turn on a new or tightened validator rule by default;
  • add a required member to ToolProvider, which is frozen within a major.

Fields are never renamed or removed within a major; a field that stops mattering is documented as ignored. The dataclass is keyword-only, so adding a field to OCTool never breaks construction.

Envelope subclasses. A consumer may subclass a result envelope or ArtifactRef. The field names role and source are reserved for octools itself: ArtifactRef defines role, so an ArtifactRef subclass uses it rather than a field of its own, and no subclass declares either name. A consumer's own subclass fields carry a consumer prefix (<pkg>_...) unless the field is being proposed upstream, and a subclass field that later collides with an octools field is the consumer's to rename or delete. A subclass that declares its own stop_reason or warnings can delete them and inherit the RecordsEnvelope and TabularEnvelope fields, which have the same shape. A subclass that keeps its own resumable keeps dumping it always, with it required in its output schema (see Paging).

Public API. The public API of every 1.x release is exactly the package root's __all__ in Python and the package root's export list in TypeScript. A name reachable only through a submodule carries no compatibility promise.

  • Renaming a tool: ship the old name as a descriptor with deprecated=True and meta={"alias_of": "<new name>"} pointing at the same func, for at least one major version of the library.
  • A result change that drops or retypes a field is a new tool name (list_objects_v2); there is no per-tool version string.

docs.title: The 1.x scope fence
docs.text:
Not in scope, by decision, classified by how it can still arrive:

  • Additive later, as an optional field or a converter key: timeouts, cost or latency hints, input_examples, strict / defer_loading flags, openWorldHint, icons, translated descriptions.
  • Additive only as an advisory marker, since runtime policy stays authoritative, the way the MCP safety hints already are: approval class, redaction rules.
  • Additive only as a separate optional field, never a change to func itself, since func is synchronous by contract: async variants, streaming or progress.
  • Needs a new major: non-JSON result content.
  • Closed, will not be added: per-tool version - the rename-with- alias path covers it.

The fence is amended only by a new decision record, never by a quiet field.

docs.title: Declaring an octools dependency
docs.text:
A consuming library declares a range, never a pin:

PythonTypeScript 
# pyproject.toml
dependencies = ["octools >= 1.0, < 2"]

{
  "dependencies": {
    "@opscogs/octools": ">=1.2.0 <2",
    "zod": "^4.4.0"
  }
}
  • The floor is the oldest release that carries every octools name the library uses. It rises only when the library starts using a new name, never just because a release came out.
  • The ceiling is the next major and nothing tighter: no ==, no ~=, no npm tilde (~1.2 means < 1.3), and no caret on a 0.x version (^0.3 means < 0.4), each of which reintroduces lockstep upgrades between libraries. On npm, ^1.2.0 and >=1.2.0 <2 are the same range.
  • Because every minor is additive under the contract above, the newest octools satisfies every library's floor at once, so a dependency resolver always finds one version for the whole environment. Two libraries can only conflict across a major.
  • Any code parsing an envelope it did not construct needs octools >= 1.0, the first release with read_envelope, and calls it instead of model_validate.
  • A library that sets stop_reason, reads resumable, validates a dumped list envelope with model_validate, or sets warnings on a list envelope or column_descriptions needs octools >= 1.1.
  • The first @opscogs/octools release is 1.2.0, so an npm range starts there whatever names the library uses; the 1.0 and 1.1 floors above apply to the Python package.
  • octools holds itself to the same rule for its own dependency: pydantic >= 2.12, < 3 in Python, and the peer dependency zod ^4.4.0 in TypeScript.

docs.title: Validator rules
docs.text:
validate_tool and validate_provider (validateTool, validateProvider) return a list of Finding; each finding has rule, message, tool and, for schema findings, path. Both packages report the same rules for the same descriptor.

Rule Fires when name_pattern name does not match the regex description_sentences fewer than two or more than four sentences any strict_clean rule input_schema leaves the strict subset; path is prefixed with /input_schema output_schema_escape output schema missing or open without meta["schema_escape"] artifact_envelope result_kind="artifact" but the output schema has no artifact property deprecated_alias deprecated tool without a meta["alias_of"] naming another tool alias_target_missing the alias names a tool the provider does not list unstable_order, duplicate_name all_tools() changes order between calls, or lists a name twice not_octool all_tools() contains something that is not an OCTool

docs.title: Listing tools for people
docs.text:
Version: 1.2.0 · Date: 2026-10-08

The listing helpers turn a provider's tools into a listing a person can read: a terminal command (octools list) for anyone with the Python package installed, and a small library API (summarize_provider and render_listing in Python, summarizeProvider and renderListing in TypeScript) for a library that wants the same listing inside its own CLI. Both packages render the same text, byte for byte. Nothing here changes the descriptor or the envelopes; it only reads them.

The Python package ships a demo provider, octools.example, so octools list octools.example works wherever the package is installed: a smoke test that the command runs, and a small conformant provider to read. Its tools may change in any release, and it is not part of the public API.

docs.title: The octools list command
docs.text:
The command ships with the Python package. The TypeScript package has no command of its own; a TypeScript CLI renders the same listing through renderListing (see Wiring render_listing into your own CLI).

octools list SPEC [--access ACCESS] [-o PATH|-] [--output-format FORMAT] [--pretty | --no-pretty]
python -m octools list SPEC [...]
octools --version
Option Meaning SPEC The provider to list: a module, a module:attr object or a zero-argument factory. --access ACCESS Only list tools with this access, local or remote; omitted lists every tool. -o, --output-file PATH\|- Write the listing to PATH instead of stdout; - or omitted means stdout. The file is written as UTF-8 and replaced atomically. --output-format FORMAT table, md (markdown is accepted as an alias), txt or json. Omitted, it follows the -o extension, else table. --pretty, --no-pretty Indent json output or print it on one line. The default is indented when stdout is a terminal and compact when it is piped or -o is set. -v, -V, --version Print octools <version> and exit 0.

With -o and no --output-format, the extension picks the format: .md and .markdown write md, .json writes json, .txt writes txt, and any other extension writes table. An explicit --output-format always wins. An -o whose directory does not exist or is not writable, or that names a directory, is a usage error before anything is listed. Option names are never abbreviated: --output is an unknown option, not a short form of --output-file.

SPEC names the provider to list, as package.module or package.module:attr (attr may itself be dotted, a.b). The working directory is importable, as it is under python -m, so a local module lists without installing it. Resolution:

  1. Import the module.
  2. With no :attr, the module itself is the candidate target; with :attr, resolve that attribute on it.
  3. A target that already satisfies ToolProvider (it has an all_tools method) is used as-is.
  4. Otherwise, a callable target is called with no arguments, and its return value must satisfy ToolProvider.
  5. Anything else is an error.
  6. The provider's all_tools() is called once, and every item it returns must be an OCTool.

docs.title: Exit codes and errors
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 The listing was printed or written. 1 The listing could not be read or written: a factory raised or returned a non-provider, all_tools() raised or returned a non-OCTool, or the output file could not be written. 2 Usage error: an unknown option or value, an unusable -o path, or a SPEC whose module does not import, whose attribute is missing, or that names neither a provider nor a callable. 130 Interrupted.

stdout carries the listing or nothing: on any failure it is empty. A usage error prints the command's usage and one octools list: error: <message> line to stderr; any other failure prints one error: <message> line:

$ octools list no_such_tools
usage: octools list [-h] [--access ACCESS] [-o PATH|-]
                    [--output-format FORMAT] [--pretty | --no-pretty]
                    SPEC
octools list: error: cannot import 'no_such_tools': No module named 'no_such_tools'

An all_tools() that raises reads '<SPEC>': all_tools raised <Type>: <message>. A SPEC that names a module-level all_tools function is called as a factory, and the tuple it returns is not a provider; the error names the fix:

$ octools list octools.example:all_tools
error: 'octools.example:all_tools': factory returned tuple, not a tool provider; name the module 'octools.example' to use its all_tools

When the output format is json, given or inferred from -o, stderr instead ends with exactly one JSON object on one line. type is usage for exit 2 and api_failure for exit 1; reason, status_code and details are always null, and hint carries the fix when there is one:

$ octools list octools.example:all_tools --output-format json
{"error": {"type": "api_failure", "exit_code": 1, "message": "'octools.example:all_tools': factory returned tuple, not a tool provider", "reason": null, "status_code": null, "details": null, "hint": "name the module 'octools.example' to use its all_tools"}}

The machine contract is --output-format json: the listing on stdout, and nothing else there. Pipe it straight into jq:

octools list SPEC --output-format json | jq '.[].name'

docs.title: Providers that need a client
docs.text: A provider reachable as a module with a module-level all_tools() works directly. A provider whose tools need a live client or configuration to construct needs a client-less, zero-argument factory function to be listed this way - one that builds the tools without reaching a real system, for example by passing None as the injected dependency.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
table, md and txt are for a person reading a terminal or a chat reply. json is the machine-readable form, for a script or another tool to parse: a plain list of dicts, one per tool, in the same key order every time.

The examples below list the demo provider, octools.example, with four tools: echo_records (reads input back as records, one page at a time), echo (its deprecated alias), block_sizes (address block sizes) and render_badge (writes a badge image through an injected sink).

docs.title: table
docs.text:
One line per tool, columns padded to width with a two-space gutter, no header. mode is destructive when the tool's destructive hint is set, write when it is not read-only, otherwise read. A deprecated tool appends [deprecated; use <alias_of>], or [deprecated] when it names no replacement.

$ octools list octools.example
echo_records  local  read  Return each input string as one record with its position.
echo          local  read  Deprecated alias of echo_records kept for one major version. [deprecated; use echo_records]
block_sizes   local  read  Return each CIDR prefix normalized, with its length and address count.
render_badge  local  read  Render a two-part SVG badge and write it through the injected sink.

docs.title: md
docs.text:
A GitHub-flavored Markdown table over the same rows, with columns name, access, mode, result_kind, pages, deprecated, summary. pages is yes when the tool takes a cursor input, the paging convention in Descriptor and envelopes.

$ octools list octools.example --output-format md
| name         | access | mode | result_kind | pages | deprecated | summary                                                                |
| ------------ | ------ | ---- | ----------- | ----- | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| echo_records | local  | read | records     | yes   | no         | Return each input string as one record with its position.              |
| echo         | local  | read | records     | yes   | yes        | Deprecated alias of echo_records kept for one major version.           |
| block_sizes  | local  | read | records     | no    | no         | Return each CIDR prefix normalized, with its length and address count. |
| render_badge | local  | read | artifact    | no    | no         | Render a two-part SVG badge and write it through the injected sink.    |

-o tools.md writes the same table to tools.md.

docs.title: txt
docs.text:
One block per tool, blocks separated by a blank line: the name (and - <title> when the tool has one), the full description wrapped at 88 columns, an access / target / result line, a hints line (ending in pages when the tool takes a cursor input), a deprecated line when the tool is deprecated, and the tool's inputs as plain aligned columns of name, type, required and description (or inputs: none). The columns are text for a terminal, not Markdown, so a type such as string|null prints as is. The first two blocks:

$ octools list octools.example --output-format txt --access local
echo_records - Echo strings as records
  Return each input string as one record with its position. Use it to check that a tool
  round-trip works before calling anything real. Returns a records envelope; when limit
  cut the list, truncated is true and next_cursor fetches the next page.
  access: local  target: -  result: records
  hints: read-only, idempotent, pages
  inputs:
    name    type           required  description
    values  array[string]  yes       Strings to echo back, one record each.
    limit   integer        no        Maximum records to return, 1 to 100; the tool enforces it.
    cursor  string|null    no        next_cursor from a previous page; omit for the first page.

echo
  Deprecated alias of echo_records kept for one major version. Call echo_records
  instead.
  access: local  target: -  result: records
  hints: read-only, idempotent, pages
  deprecated: use echo_records
  inputs:
    name    type           required  description
    values  array[string]  yes       Strings to echo back, one record each.
    limit   integer        no        Maximum records to return, 1 to 100; the tool enforces it.
    cursor  string|null    no        next_cursor from a previous page; omit for the first page.
...

docs.title: json
docs.text:
json.dumps([summary.as_row() for summary in summaries], indent=2) with --pretty (the default on a terminal), or on one line with separators=(",", ":") otherwise; one flat dict per tool (the first shown here):

$ octools list octools.example --output-format json --pretty
[
  {
    "name": "echo_records",
    "title": "Echo strings as records",
    "summary": "Return each input string as one record with its position.",
    "description": "Return each input string as one record with its position. Use it to check that a tool round-trip works before calling anything real. Returns a records envelope; when limit cut the list, truncated is true and next_cursor fetches the next page.",
    "access": "local",
    "target": null,
    "result_kind": "records",
    "read_only": true,
    "destructive": false,
    "idempotent": true,
    "pages": true,
    "deprecated": false,
    "alias_of": null,
    "inputs": [
      {
        "name": "values",
        "type": "array[string]",
        "required": true,
        "description": "Strings to echo back, one record each."
      },
      {
        "name": "limit",
        "type": "integer",
        "required": false,
        "description": "Maximum records to return, 1 to 100; the tool enforces it."
      },
      {
        "name": "cursor",
        "type": "string|null",
        "required": false,
        "description": "next_cursor from a previous page; omit for the first page."
      }
    ]
  },
  ...
]

docs.title: Library API
docs.text: Both packages export the pieces above so a producer's own CLI can render the same listing without shelling out to octools list. The TypeScript names are camelCase: summarizeTool, summarizeProvider, renderMarkdownTable, renderListing.

docs.title: ToolSummary and InputSummary
docs.text:
summarize_tool(tool) returns a ToolSummary: name, title, summary (the first sentence of description, or the whole description when no sentence boundary is found), description, access, target, result_kind, read_only, destructive, idempotent, pages (true when the input schema's properties include cursor), deprecated, alias_of (the tool's meta["alias_of"] when it is a non-empty string, else None), and inputs, a tuple of InputSummary. In TypeScript the ToolSummary properties are camelCase (resultKind, readOnly, aliasOf) and inputs is a readonly array.

Each InputSummary describes one property of the tool's input schema: name, type (rendered from the property's JSON Schema, see below), required, and description (the property's own description when it is a string, else None). Inputs are read in the schema's own property order.

ToolSummary.as_row() (asRow()) returns a flat, JSON-ready dict in a fixed key order - name, title, summary, description, access, target, result_kind, read_only, destructive, idempotent, pages, deprecated, alias_of, inputs (each input as a dict of name, type, required, description) - the shape the json format serializes. The row keys are the same snake_case keys in both packages.

Type rendering never raises, for any input mapping:

Property shape Rendered type "type": "string" string "type" is a list member types joined with \| (string\|null) "type": "array" with "items" array[<items type>] "enum" present, with or without "type" enum(a\|b\|c); past 40 characters, the values that fit then \|... "const" const(<value>) "$ref" the last path segment (#/$defs/Mode -> Mode) "anyOf" or "oneOf" member types joined with \| (enum(a\|b)\|null) anything else any

enum and const take precedence over the other keys, since their values are what a reader needs. A string value renders bare and any other value as JSON (enum(null|true|1.5)).

docs.title: summarize_provider
render_markdown_table and render_listing
Wiring render_listing into your own CLI
docs.text:
A library that already ships a CLI can add its own tools list command by delegating straight to render_listing (renderListing), instead of building rows by hand:

PythonTypeScript 
import argparse

from octools import LISTING_STYLES, render_listing
from octools import example as my_tools


def cmd_tools_list(args: argparse.Namespace) -> None:
    text = render_listing(my_tools, style=args.output_format, access=args.access)
    print(text, end="")


parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
subcommands = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command")
tools_list = subcommands.add_parser("tools-list")
tools_list.add_argument(
    "--output-format",
    metavar="FORMAT",
    choices=LISTING_STYLES,
    default="table",
    help="Render the listing in this format.",
)
tools_list.add_argument(
    "--access",
    metavar="ACCESS",
    choices=["local", "remote"],
    help="Only list tools with this access.",
)
tools_list.set_defaults(func=cmd_tools_list)

import { parseArgs } from "node:util";

import {
  ACCESS_KINDS,
  LISTING_STYLES,
  type Access,
  type ListingStyle,
  renderListing,
} from "@opscogs/octools";
import * as myTools from "./my_tools.js";

function oneOf<T extends string>(
  value: string | undefined,
  allowed: readonly T[],
  option: string,
): T | undefined {
  if (value !== undefined && !(allowed as readonly string[]).includes(value)) {
    throw new RangeError(`${option} must be one of ${allowed.join(", ")}`);
  }
  return value as T | undefined;
}

export function cmdToolsList(args: string[]): void {
  const { values } = parseArgs({
    args,
    options: {
      "output-format": { type: "string", default: "table" },
      access: { type: "string" },
    },
  });
  const style: ListingStyle | undefined = oneOf(
    values["output-format"],
    LISTING_STYLES,
    "--output-format",
  );
  const access: Access | undefined = oneOf(
    values.access,
    ACCESS_KINDS,
    "--access",
  );
  process.stdout.write(renderListing(myTools, { style, access }));
}

Every producer's tools list command then supports the same four formats with no per-library formatting code, and stays in sync with the descriptor whenever a tool's description, hints or inputs change.

docs.title: The TypeScript package
docs.text:
Version: 1.2.0 · Date: 2026-10-08

@opscogs/octools is octools for TypeScript and JavaScript. It covers the whole public API of the Python package: the OCTool descriptor, the result envelopes and their tolerant reader, the validators, the MCP and Anthropic converters, the listing helpers, the schema helpers, and the vocabularies, fallbacks and constants. Both packages pass the same spec/ conformance fixtures and are released together at the same version (see One contract, two languages).

Every page of this site shows each example in both languages. This page covers what is specific to TypeScript: the runtime, the names, schemas from zod, and the few places where the two languages behave differently. The generated TypeScript API reference documents every export.

docs.title: Install and runtime
docs.text:
npm install @opscogs/octools zod
  • Node 22.18 or newer. The package declares engines.node >= 22.18.0.
  • ESM only. Load it with import; there is no CommonJS build, so a CommonJS module uses a dynamic import(). Type declarations ship in the package.
  • zod 4 is a peer dependency (^4.4.0) and the only runtime dependency, so the zod your project already uses is the one the envelopes and schema helpers run on. Import it as import * as z from "zod".
  • No SDK. The package never depends on @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @anthropic-ai/sdk or openai; the converters return plain objects.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
API names follow TypeScript idiom: functions and fields in camelCase, types in PascalCase, constants in upper snake case. Wire keys never change: every key a descriptor, envelope, finding, listing row or converter emits or reads is spelled exactly as the spec spells it (column_kinds, next_cursor, inputSchema, result_kind). Each name maps one to one onto a name in the Python package's __all__:

Python TypeScript OCTool(name=..., input_schema=..., ...) new OCTool({ name, inputSchema, ... }), every field in camelCase ToolProvider (all_tools()) interface ToolProvider (allTools()) RecordsEnvelope[T] RecordsEnvelope(item), a zod schema; type RecordsEnvelope<T> TabularEnvelope, ArtifactEnvelope, ArtifactRef the same names: a zod schema and its output type Model.model_validate(data) Model.parse(data) read_envelope, validate_tabular readEnvelope, validateTabular records_schema, tabular_schema, artifact_schema recordsSchema, tabularSchema, artifactSchema schema_for(Model, mode=...), input_schema_for, output_schema_for schemaFor(schema, { io }), inputSchemaFor, outputSchemaFor, taking zod schemas strict_clean, strip_keys(schema, keys=..., prefixes=...) strictClean, stripKeys(schema, { keys, prefixes }) strip_titles, close_objects stripTitles, closeObjects NoTitleGenerator none: schemaFor strips titles itself validate_tool, validate_provider, count_sentences validateTool, validateProvider, countSentences merge_providers, check_tool_listing mergeProviders, checkToolListing to_mcp_tool(tool, name_prefix=...), to_anthropic_tool toMcpTool(tool, { namePrefix }), toAnthropicTool summarize_tool, summarize_provider(provider, access=...) summarizeTool, summarizeProvider(provider, { access }) render_listing(provider, style=..., access=..., pretty=...) renderListing(provider, { style, access, pretty }) render_markdown_table, ToolSummary.as_row(), InputSummary renderMarkdownTable, ToolSummary.asRow(), InputSummary Cell, ColumnKind, ColumnScale, Sensitivity the same type names Access, ResultKind, ListingStyle the same type names Finding, OCToolError the same class names constants such as SPEC_VERSION, COLUMN_KINDS, NAME_RE the same names

The *_RE constants are RegExp objects, the STRICT_* sets are ReadonlySet<string>, and the vocabulary values are readonly arrays. Keyword arguments become one options object ({ namePrefix }, { access }, { style, access, pretty }). The public API is exactly the package root's export list; a module path inside the package carries no compatibility promise.

docs.title: Schemas from zod
docs.text:
The schema helpers take zod schemas where the Python helpers take pydantic models, and emit the same JSON Schema 2020-12 dialect and the same strict-clean output. zod metadata plays the role of pydantic field extras:

  • .describe("...") or .meta({ description }) sets a field's description.
  • .meta({ "x-sensitivity": "identifier" }) on a result field emits the x-sensitivity extension key.
  • .meta({ format: "date-time" }) on a z.string() emits a format.
  • .meta({ id: "Name" }) on a model puts it in $defs under that name wherever it is nested and refers to it by $ref, as pydantic does for every nested model. The envelopes carry their own ids, so a TabularEnvelope field in an argument model becomes {"$ref": "#/$defs/TabularEnvelope"}.

inputSchemaFor closes every object with additionalProperties: false. outputSchemaFor keeps each object as the schema declares it: a z.object stays open, as a pydantic model does by default, and a z.strictObject is closed. A schema describes what a parse accepts (the wire shape), so a .default() over a schema with a transform states its default only as .prefault().

There is no NoTitleGenerator: the Python class exists only to steer pydantic's schema generator, and schemaFor removes every title itself.

docs.title: Envelopes are parses
docs.text:
Each envelope is a zod schema whose output type has the same name. TabularEnvelope.parse(data) is the strict producer path: an unknown key or vocabulary value throws ZodError, and the value it returns is the envelope's wire form, ready for JSON.stringify, with unset optional fields left out and resumable present only on a truncated list. readEnvelope(model, data) is the tolerant reader for an envelope from another process, with the same fallbacks as Python's read_envelope (see Reading envelopes from another process).

import { TabularEnvelope, readEnvelope, validateTabular } from "@opscogs/octools";

const result = TabularEnvelope.parse({
  columns: ["host", "hits"],
  column_kinds: ["fqdn", "integer"],
  rows: [["a.demo.example", 3]],
  row_count: 1,
  truncated: false,
});
validateTabular(result); // []

const read = readEnvelope(TabularEnvelope, JSON.stringify(result));

docs.title: Language differences
docs.text:
Both packages pass every spec/ fixture, so they agree on everything the fixtures pin down. Where JavaScript and Python differ underneath, the packages differ as follows.

Topic Python octools TypeScript @opscogs/octools JSON 1.0 and 1 1.0 stays a float: a 1.0 cell fails the integer and big_integer kinds JSON.parse reads both as the number 1: an integral cell fits integer and big_integer however it was written Integers above 2^53 − 1 Read exactly in every integer field and cell An integer field (count, row_count, total_count, bytes, width, height) beyond it fails the parse; a numeric cell is already rounded by JSON.parse Type coercion pydantic's lax mode converts "3" to 3 and "false" to false No coercion: a value of the wrong JSON type throws ZodError, in .parse and in readEnvelope Bytes in readEnvelope UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32, detected A Uint8Array is decoded as UTF-8, the JSON wire encoding, only; UTF-16 or UTF-32 bytes fail to read String formats in schemas A pydantic format emits format only A zod format such as z.iso.datetime() also emits a pattern, which strictClean reports in an input schema; use z.string().meta({ format: "date-time" }) Foreign items in a listing Labelled with Python type names: <int>, <str>, <NoneType>, <list> Labelled with JavaScript type names: <number>, <string>, <null>, <array> Schema helpers Take pydantic models; field extras via json_schema_extra Take zod schemas; field extras via .meta() NoTitleGenerator Exported No counterpart

What these mean in practice:

  • Send big integers as strings. total_count and big_integer cells accept a decimal string, which both languages read exactly. A TypeScript reader cannot recover an integer cell beyond 2^53 − 1 that arrived as a JSON number, because the rounding happens in JSON.parse before octools sees the value.
  • Send the right JSON types. An envelope a Python reader accepts through coercion ("count": "3") fails in TypeScript. A producer's own strict parse in its tests catches this, in either language.
  • Foreign-item labels appear in not_octool messages and in the tool field of a duplicate_name finding raised over two non-tool items, so a test that asserts on that tool value is language-specific.

Errors are JavaScript errors: OCToolError extends Error, an envelope that fails a parse throws ZodError, malformed JSON text throws SyntaxError, and renderListing throws RangeError for an unknown style where Python raises ValueError.

The octools list command and the octools.example demo provider ship with the Python package only. A TypeScript CLI renders the same listing with renderListing (see Listing tools for people).
